blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Events A and B are independent if and only if P(A|B) = P(A). Equivalently, P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: A and B are independent when learning that B happened tells you nothing new about A. The two forms of the definition are the same statement. Substitute P(A|B) = P(A) into the general multiplication rule of §5.3 and you get the product form.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Two flips of a fair coin are independent: a head on the first does not change the chance of a head on the second. In the NCD clinic, P(D) × P(H) = 0.2 × 0.3 = 0.06, but P(D and H) = 0.1. The product does not match, so diabetes and hypertension are not independent there: P(H|D) = 0.5 is higher than P(H) = 0.3. Whether the events “systolic BP ≥ 140 mmHg” and “salt intake above 5 g/day” are independent in a given population is settled the same way: compare P(BP ≥ 140 | high salt) with P(BP ≥ 140) in the data.

points.html: Test: independent if and only if P(A|B) = P(A), equivalently P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

Independence and mutual exclusivity are different, and they are often confused. Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen (P(A and B) = 0). Two mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are therefore always dependent: learning that one happened tells you the other did not.

Many methods later in the book assume that observations are independent of one another. Treating repeated measurements on the same patient, or children in the same household, as independent is a frequent and serious error in applied research; clustered data need methods that allow for the within-cluster correlation (§15.2).

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between “mutually exclusive” and “independent” using a concrete pair of events.
questions.answer: Mutually exclusive events cannot both happen: one person’s ABO blood group being A and being B. Independent events can both happen but do not change each other’s probability: two unrelated patients in different villages each testing positive for malaria. Mutually exclusive events with non-zero probabilities are in fact dependent: knowing the blood group is A tells you with certainty it is not B.

questions.prompt: How does conditional probability define independence?
questions.answer: A and B are independent exactly when P(A|B) = P(A): learning that B happened leaves the probability of A unchanged. Equivalently P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B).

questions.prompt: In an under-five clinic, P(underweight) = 0.25, P(recent diarrhoea) = 0.20 and P(both) = 0.08. Find P(underweight | recent diarrhoea). Are the two events independent? Show the check.
questions.answer: P(U|D) = P(U and D) ÷ P(D) = 0.08 ÷ 0.20 = 0.40. This is not equal to P(U) = 0.25, so the events are not independent. The product check agrees: P(U) × P(D) = 0.25 × 0.20 = 0.05 ≠ 0.08. Underweight is more common among children with recent diarrhoea than overall. (This is an association; the data do not say which causes which.)
